prior_approach.content: Different irradiation methods have previously been used to create quantum emitters in hBN, including lasers, ions, neutrons, and electrons.
prior_approach.evidence_span: It has already been shown that different kinds of irradiation can be used to create quantum emitters in hBN, including lasers [19], ions [20], neutrons [21] and electrons [11, 22].

prior_approach.content: Direct correlations between irradiation and atomic structure were previously established only for electron irradiation in monolayer hBN and high-energy He+ ions in multilayer hBN.
prior_approach.evidence_span: So far, only in the case of electrons in monolayer hBN [23, 24], and high energy ions (500 kV He+) for multilayer hBN [25] has a direct correlation between irradiation and the exact atomic structure been established

prior_approach.content: Analytical-potential molecular dynamics simulations predicted that low-energy noble-gas ions should create defects efficiently.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Analytical potential molecular dynamics simulations have shown that low-energy noble-gas ions should have high de- fect creation efficiencies.

prior_approach.content: Lehtinen et al. predicted defect yields and probabilities for 100 eV Ar irradiation in monolayer hBN.
prior_approach.evidence_span: In an earlier work, Lehtinen et al. [28] predicted that about 0.8 defects are created per 100 eV Ar ion with roughly equal probabilities (∼0.2) for creating boron (VB) and nitrogen single vacancies (VN) and roughly twice that for double vacancies (VBN) in monolayer hBN.

prior_approach.evidence_span: Ghaderzadeh et al. [27], on the other hand, reported about 0.2 defects being created per 150 eV Ar ion at low fluences. They predict a higher density of VN (∼0.4) than for VBN (∼0.3) and VB (∼0.2).

prior_approach.evidence_span: For electron irradiation, it was experimentally shown that intermediate electron energies (60–100 keV) are more likely to displace boron than nitrogen [23].

prior_approach.content: The only prior direct experimental comparison to low-energy ion-irradiation simulations for monolayer hBN was in Refs. 31 and 32.

causal_claim.content: Ion irradiation created defects dominated by boron single vacancies and also double vacancies.
causal_claim.evidence_span: we predominantly observe boron single vacancies after ion irradiation, followed by double vacancies at half the count.

causal_claim.content: Si and C impurity filling of vacancies may hinder selective creation of quantum emitters in hBN.
causal_claim.evidence_span: vacancy filling with Si and C impurity atoms plays a more significant role in the created defects than previously assumed, potentially posing a problem for selective creation of quantum emitters in hBN.

causal_claim.content: Electron irradiation in low-pressure oxygen preferentially removes boron and often produces nitrogen-terminated pores.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Electron irradiation in a low-pressure oxygen atmosphere has also been shown to result in preferential removal of boron, at least from pore edges [24], often leading to nitrogen-terminated pores.

causal_claim.content: The chosen defect density confirms irradiation damage while keeping repeated ion impacts on the same site rare.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This defect density is sufficiently high to confirm irradiation-related damage yet low enough that most ions encounter pristine hBN, ensuring that ions rarely impact the exact same location more than once.

causal_claim.content: Vacancy filling by impurities appears to be an uncontrollable by-product of ion irradiation.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This vacancy filling appears to be an uncontrollable by-product of ion irradiation.

causal_claim.content: Lower-energy ions produce defects more efficiently than higher-energy ions because the displacement cross section is larger at lower energies.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This also confirms that defect production is much more efficient with <1 keV ions compared to >20 keV ions, as would be expected from the larger displacement cross sec- tion at lower energies.

mechanism_principle.content: Greater defect production efficiency at lower ion energies is explained by a larger displacement cross section.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: as would be expected from the larger displacement cross sec- tion at lower energies.

mechanism_principle.evidence_span: that relies on atomic number (Z)-contrast [43] to differentiate between atoms and defects in the images

mechanism_principle.content: Intrinsic defects may arise from unavoidable beam damage or pre-existing defects from growth, preparation, or cleaning.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: that could be explained, at least in part, by unavoidable electron-beam-induced defects along with the possibility of intrinsic defects being present in the material either from the growth or introduced during the sample preparation or cleaning procedure.

mechanism_principle.content: Not all pre-irradiation defects came from imaging because many are larger defects unlikely to form in a single image acquisition.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span:
We note, however, that it is unlikely
that all recorded pre-irradiation defects are introduced by the

mechanism_principle.content: Defective hBN may be easier to damage than pristine hBN.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span:
another explana-
tion could be that it is easier to damage a defective material
than a pristine one, as reported in Ref. [49].

mechanism_principle.content: An ion must strike within about two unit cells of an existing defect to enlarge it; otherwise it likely creates a new defect in pristine hBN.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span:
if a subsequent
ion was to impinge on hBN it would have to be within two
unit cells (twice the lattice constant, i.e., 0.5 nm) of an exist-
ing defect in order to possibly enlarge that defect. If it im-
pacted further away, it would encounter pristine hBN possi-
bly creating a new defect.

mechanism_principle.content: If defects are charged, they can influence bonding and charge transfer beyond two unit cells, potentially changing displacement thresholds even when a new defect forms.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span:
However, if the existing defects are charged [55],
their influence on the defect creation process can reach further
away than the two unit cells due to their influence on the local
bonding environment as well as charge transfer between the
incoming ion and the lattice. Hence, there may be changes to
the displacement threshold energy even when the ion impact
leads to the creation of a new defect.

mechanism_principle.content: Adjacent atoms should be dimmer because missing-neighbor probe-tail scattering and increased vibrational smearing lower their intensity.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span:
atoms adja-
cent to a vacancy should exhibit slightly lower intensities due
to the missing probe-tail scattering contribution from the ab-
sent neighbouring atom [56], and increased vibrational smear-
ing of the under-coordinated edge atoms.

mechanism_principle.content: If knock-on damage and displacement cross sections were the same in graphene and hBN, similar defect sizes would be expected.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span:
Assuming the same knock-on type of
irradiation damage (and displacement cross-sections) for both
materials, one would expect a similar defect size to be created
in both cases.

mechanism_principle.content: Atoms next to edges usually look dimmer because probe tails collect less neighboring scattering and under-coordinated edge atoms move more, smearing intensity.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span:
Such a reduction in intensity is
mainly attributed to two effects: First, the electron probe does not consist solely of a bright central maximum but also exhibits
so-called probe tails, which interact with the atomic potential beyond the immediate probe position. These probe tails arise due to
several physical effects, including finite convergence angle–related Airy disks, as well as spherical and higher-order aberrations.
In practice, this means that the ADF detector records scattering not only from the atom directly at the probe position but also
from neighboring atoms. Atoms located next to edges or vacancies have fewer neighboring atoms, leading to reduced scattering
and consequently lower detected intensities. Second, atoms at edges or vacancies are under-coordinated and therefore can move
more freely in comparison to atoms within the pristine lattice, resulting in a more smeared-out appearance and lower measured
intensity in the ADF-STEM images.

mechanism_principle.content: Oxygen is proposed as the likely species because it is slightly heavier than nitrogen, present in hydrocarbon contamination, and more chemically plausible and abundant than alternatives like fluorine.

intensities, as it is only slightly heavier than nitrogen, is present in hydrocarbon contamination [67], and is chemically more
likely, and far more abundant, to substitute nitrogen than neighbouring elements such as fluorine.

mechanism_principle.content: To enlarge an existing defect, a subsequent ion likely must strike within about two unit cells of that defect; otherwise it more likely creates a new defect in pristine hBN. bly creating a new defect.

away than the two unit cells due to their influence on the local
bonding environment as well as charge transfer between the
incoming ion and the lattice. Hence, there may be changes to
the displacement threshold energy even when the ion impact

mechanism_principle.content: Atoms adjacent to vacancies or edges appear dimmer in ADF-STEM because they receive less neighboring probe-tail scattering and, being under-coordinated, undergo greater vibrational smearing.
evidence_spans:
atoms adja-
cent to a vacancy should exhibit slightly lower intensities due
to the missing probe-tail scattering contribution from the ab-
sent neighbouring atom [56], and increased vibrational smear-
ing of the under-coordinated edge atoms.

Such a reduction in intensity is
mainly attributed to two effects: First, the electron probe does not consist solely of a bright central maximum but also exhibits
so-called probe tails, which interact with the atomic potential beyond the immediate probe position. These probe tails arise due to
several physical effects, including finite convergence angle–related Airy disks, as well as spherical and higher-order aberrations.
In practice, this means that the ADF detector records scattering not only from the atom directly at the probe position but also
from neighboring atoms. Atoms located next to edges or vacancies have fewer neighboring atoms, leading to reduced scattering
and consequently lower detected intensities. Second, atoms at edges or vacancies are under-coordinated and therefore can move
more freely in comparison to atoms within the pristine lattice, resulting in a more smeared-out appearance and lower measured
intensity in the ADF-STEM images.

evidence_result.content: Oxygen adatoms show no significant preference between boron and nitrogen single vacancies.

evidence_result.content: At double vacancies, carbon relaxes into the boron site, while oxygen prefers the nitrogen site.
evidence_result.evidence_span: In the case of a double vacancy, a carbon adatom will always relax into the vacant boron site, resulting in an apparent nitrogen vacancy, whereas oxygen prefers the vacant nitrogen site, although not exclusively.

contradiction.content: The experimental defect distribution in irradiated hBN contradicts analytical-potential MD and related simulation predictions: experiments predominantly observe boron single vacancies, with fewer double vacancies, whereas prior computations predicted either similar VB/VN formation with more double vacancies, a predominance of VN, or no significant B/N ejection difference.
evidence_spans: Contrary to what analytical potential molecular dynamics simulations have predicted, we predominantly observe boron single vacancies after ion irradiation, followed by double vacancies at half the count.
Interestingly, these results do not align with the predicted defect distributions reported by the simulation studies [27, 28].
Contrary to our experimental results, but in agreement with other simulation studies [27, 28], we find no significant difference in the ejection of B or N atoms from the lattice
Our experimental results are, however, in clear contra- diction with theoretical studies based on analytical-potential molecular-dynamics simulations

Our results challenge earlier computational work predicting either similar formation probabilities for VN and VB and a higher probability for VBN [28], or a predominance for VN over VB and VBN under Ar irradiation at similar energies [27].

contradiction.content: The simulation–experiment discrepancy cannot be explained by vacancy filling masking nitrogen vacancies, because post-irradiation impurity atoms predominantly occupy boron sites; together with the observed excess of boron vacancies, this indicates simulations do not fully capture defect creation dynamics.
evidence_spans: Contrary to the limited number of impurity atom substitutions reported in Refs. [31, 32], these post-irradiation impurity atoms predomi- nantly occupy boron sites, hence ruling out the possibility that the discrepancy between simulations and experiments could be explained by vacancy filling that obscures the number of nitrogen single vacancies created by the irradiation.
Since we experimentally observe more boron single vacancies and also more impurity atom filling of boron sites, the simulations are unable to fully capture the defect creation dynamics.
